notes.definition: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Changes of state happen at the melting point (melting and freezing) and the boiling point (boiling and condensing), and the energy needed depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.
explanation: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Melting and freezing take place at the melting point; boiling and condensing take place at the boiling point. The three states can be represented by a simple model in which the particles are small solid spheres. In a solid the particles are close together in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid the particles are still close together (mostly touching) but are arranged randomly and can move around each other. In a gas the particles are far apart, arranged randomly and move quickly in all directions.

Particle theory explains changes of state in terms of energy transfers. When a solid is heated, its particles gain energy and vibrate more. At the melting point the particles have enough energy to overcome some of the forces between them, and the solid melts. When a liquid is heated to its boiling point, the particles have enough energy to overcome the remaining forces and they separate, forming a gas. Freezing and condensing are the reverse: energy is transferred to the surroundings and the forces between particles pull them back together.

The amount of energy needed to change state from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas depends on the strength of the forces between the particles of the substance. The nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance: they may be ions (ionic compounds), atoms (metals and giant covalent structures) or molecules (small molecules). The stronger the forces between the particles, the higher the melting point and boiling point. For example, sodium chloride has strong ionic bonds and melts at 801 °C, while oxygen molecules have only weak forces between them and oxygen boils at −183 °C.

You can predict the state of a substance at a given temperature from its melting point and boiling point. Below the melting point the substance is a solid. Between the melting point and the boiling point it is a liquid. Above the boiling point it is a gas. For example, bromine melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C, so at 25 °C it is a liquid and at 80 °C it is a gas. Remember that negative temperatures are colder: −50 °C is lower than −7 °C.

Individual atoms do not have the bulk properties of materials. Properties such as melting point, boiling point, colour, hardness and electrical conductivity belong to large numbers of particles together and depend on how they are arranged and bonded. A single copper atom does not conduct electricity or have a melting point, and a single bromine molecule is not a red-brown liquid. These are properties of the substance, not of one particle.
keyFacts: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Melting and freezing happen at the melting point; boiling and condensing happen at the boiling point.
Solid: regular, touching, vibrating. Liquid: random, touching, moving around each other. Gas: random, far apart, moving quickly.
Melting and boiling need energy to be transferred to the substance; freezing and condensing transfer energy to the surroundings.
The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.
The type of particle (ion, atom or molecule) depends on the bonding and structure.
Stronger forces between particles mean higher melting and boiling points.
Below mp: solid. Between mp and bp: liquid. Above bp: gas.
Atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials.

keyTerms.definition: The temperature at which a solid melts and a liquid freezes.
The temperature at which a liquid boils and a gas condenses.
The change of state from solid to liquid.
The change of state from liquid to solid.
The change of state from liquid to gas, throughout the liquid, at the boiling point.
The change of state from gas to liquid.
A model in which the particles of a substance are represented as small solid spheres.
Properties of a material as a whole, such as melting point or conductivity, which individual atoms do not have.

workedExamples.title: Predicting states from data
workedExamples.question: Chlorine has a melting point of −101 °C and a boiling point of −34 °C. Predict its state at (a) −120 °C, (b) −50 °C, (c) 20 °C.
steps: (a) −120 °C is below the melting point (−101 °C), so chlorine is a solid.
(b) −50 °C is above the melting point (−101 °C) but below the boiling point (−34 °C), so it is a liquid.
(c) 20 °C is above the boiling point (−34 °C), so it is a gas.

workedExamples.title: Temperature range of the liquid state
workedExamples.question: Ethanol melts at −114 °C and boils at 78 °C. Over what range of temperature is ethanol a liquid, and how wide is this range?
steps: Ethanol is a liquid between its melting point and boiling point: −114 °C to 78 °C.
Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding: 78 + 114 = 192 °C.

workedExamples.title: Explaining different melting points
workedExamples.question: Explain why magnesium oxide (melting point 2852 °C) has a much higher melting point than water (0 °C).
steps: Melting needs energy to overcome the forces between particles.
Magnesium oxide is ionic: there are strong electrostatic forces between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions throughout a giant lattice.
Water is made of small molecules with weak forces between the molecules.
Much more energy is needed to overcome the strong forces in magnesium oxide.
workedExamples.answer: The forces between ions in MgO are much stronger than the forces between water molecules, so far more energy is needed to melt it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think particles in a solid do not move.
misconceptions.right: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; they move more as the temperature rises.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the particles in a liquid are far apart.
misconceptions.right: Liquid particles are close together (mostly touching) but arranged randomly and able to move around each other.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think particles expand or melt when a substance is heated.
misconceptions.right: The particles themselves do not change. They gain energy and move more; individual particles do not have bulk properties like melting.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think −20 °C is higher than −10 °C.
misconceptions.right: With negative temperatures, the larger number is colder: −20 °C is lower than −10 °C.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think covalent bonds break when a molecular substance boils.
misconceptions.right: For small molecules only the weak forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds stay intact.

realWorld: Gallium melts at about 30 °C, so a piece of gallium melts in your hand, while tungsten (melting point 3422 °C) is used where very high temperatures are needed.
Road salt lowers the freezing point of water on roads in winter, so ice melts even below 0 °C.
Liquid nitrogen (boiling point −196 °C) is used to freeze and store biological samples.
higherTier: Limitations of the simple particle model: in the model there are no forces between the particles, all particles are represented as spheres, and the spheres are solid (and inelastic).
Because the model has no forces, it cannot explain why energy is needed to melt or boil a substance, or why different substances have different melting and boiling points.
Real particles are not solid spheres: atoms are mostly empty space, molecules have different shapes, and ions and molecules can be different sizes.
examTips: For 'predict the state' questions, compare the temperature with BOTH the melting point and boiling point, and take care with negative numbers.
Link melting point to energy and forces: 'stronger forces between particles, so more energy needed to overcome them, so higher melting point'.
Name the type of particle and force: ions (ionic bonds), atoms (covalent bonds or metallic bonds) or molecules (intermolecular forces).
Higher tier: the three limitations of the particle model are no forces, all particles spheres, and spheres are solid.
Use 'particles vibrate' for solids, never 'particles don't move'.
summary: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Melting and freezing occur at the melting point; boiling and condensing at the boiling point.
The simple model shows particles as small solid spheres.
Energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between particles.
Stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points.
Atoms themselves do not have bulk properties.
Higher: the model's limitations are no forces, all particles spheres, and solid spheres.

questions.explanation: Gas to liquid is condensing. Freezing is liquid to solid; melting is solid to liquid.

questions.question: At which temperature does a substance freeze?
markScheme: 1 mark: Its melting point
questions.explanation: Freezing happens at the same temperature as melting: the melting point. Only water freezes at 0 °C.

questions.question: Which statement describes the particles in a liquid?
options: Close together and vibrating in fixed positions
Far apart and in a regular pattern
Close together and able to move around each other
markScheme: 1 mark: Close together and able to move around each other
questions.explanation: Liquid particles are close together but randomly arranged and can move past each other.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of iron.
What is the state of iron at 2000 °C?
markScheme: 1 mark: Liquid
questions.explanation: 2000 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point, so iron is a liquid.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of oxygen.
What is the state of oxygen at −200 °C?
markScheme: 1 mark: Liquid
questions.explanation: −200 °C is warmer than −218 °C (melting point) but colder than −183 °C (boiling point), so oxygen is a liquid.

questions.question: Which substance is most likely to have the highest melting point?
options: A substance with weak forces between its particles
A substance whose particles are small molecules
A substance with very strong forces between its particles
A substance that is a gas at room temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: A substance with very strong forces between its particles
questions.explanation: The stronger the forces between particles, the more energy needed to separate them and the higher the melting point.

questions.question: What happens to the particles of a solid as it is heated to its melting point?
options: They gain energy and vibrate more until they can move around each other.
They lose energy and stop moving.
markScheme: 1 mark: They gain energy and vibrate more until they can move around each other.
questions.explanation: Heating transfers energy to the particles, so they vibrate more. At the melting point they can overcome some forces and move around each other. The particles do not expand or melt themselves.

questions.question: Which statement about a single atom of copper is correct?
options: It has a melting point of 1085 °C.
It does not have the bulk properties of copper metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: It does not have the bulk properties of copper metal.
questions.explanation: Bulk properties such as conductivity, melting point and lustre belong to a large number of atoms bonded together, not to individual atoms.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of bromine.
Calculate the range of temperatures over which bromine is a liquid.
questions.explanation: Range = boiling point − melting point = 59 − (−7) = 59 + 7 = 66 °C.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of methane.
Calculate the range of temperatures over which methane is a liquid.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 20 °C
questions.explanation: −162 − (−182) = −162 + 182 = 20 °C. Check: counting up from −182 to −162 is 20 degrees.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of mercury.
Calculate the range of temperatures over which mercury is a liquid.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 396 °C
questions.explanation: 357 + 39 = 396 °C. Mercury's wide liquid range is why it was used in thermometers.

questions.question:
A substance is a liquid over a temperature range of 192 °C.
The boiling point of the substance is 78 °C.
Calculate the melting point of the substance.
markScheme: 1 mark: melting point = boiling point − range
questions.explanation: Range = bp − mp, so mp = bp − range = 78 − 192 = −114 °C (this is ethanol). Check: 78 − (−114) = 192.

questions.question:
Name the change of state that happens at the boiling point when:
(a) a liquid is heated
(b) a gas is cooled
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) boiling
1 mark: (b) condensing
questions.explanation: Both boiling and condensing take place at the boiling point.

questions.question: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a gas.
markScheme: 1 mark: far apart / randomly arranged
1 mark: moving quickly in all directions
questions.explanation: Gas particles have the most energy and are widely spaced.

questions.question: State how the particles are represented in the simple particle model.
markScheme: 1 mark: as small solid spheres
questions.explanation: The model uses small, solid spheres for all particles (atoms, ions or molecules).

questions.question: Explain, in terms of particles and energy, what happens when ice melts.
markScheme: 1 mark: (water) particles gain energy / vibrate more
1 mark: some forces between particles are overcome so particles can move around each other
questions.explanation: Energy transferred to the ice allows the particles to break out of their fixed positions.

questions.question: Explain why different substances have different melting points.
markScheme: 1 mark: the forces between particles have different strengths (because of different bonding/structure)
1 mark: stronger forces need more energy to overcome, giving a higher melting point
questions.explanation: The type of particle and bonding determines the strength of the forces.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points and boiling points of three substances, A, B and C.
Give the state of each substance at 25 °C.
markScheme: 1 mark: A liquid
1 mark: B solid
1 mark: C gas
questions.explanation: A: 25 is between −95 and 56 (liquid). B: 25 is below 801 (solid). C: 25 is above −196 (gas).

questions.question:
Name the type of particle present in:
(a) sodium chloride
(b) water.
State which substance has stronger forces between its particles.

markScheme: 1 mark: there are no forces between the particles
1 mark: all particles are represented as spheres
1 mark: the spheres are solid (inelastic)
questions.explanation: These are the three limitations named in the specification. Real particles attract each other, have different shapes and are not solid.

questions.question: Explain why the simple particle model, with solid inelastic spheres and no forces, cannot explain why energy is needed to melt a solid.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy is needed to overcome the forces (of attraction) between particles when melting
1 mark: the model has no forces, so it gives no reason why energy is needed / why melting points differ
questions.explanation: In reality melting needs energy to overcome attractions. A model without forces cannot account for this or for differences in melting point.

questions.question: A student says: 'Bromine is a red-brown liquid, so each bromine molecule is red-brown and liquid.' Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: colour and state are bulk properties of the substance
1 mark: they depend on large numbers of particles and how they are arranged; a single molecule does not have them
questions.explanation: Atoms and molecules do not have bulk properties such as state, colour or melting point.

questions.question: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases, and explain what happens to the particles when a liquid boils.
markScheme: Indicative content: solid: regular, close together, vibrate in fixed positions; liquid: random, close together, move around each other; gas: random, far apart, move quickly in all directions; boiling: liquid heated, particles gain energy, move faster; at the boiling point the particles have enough energy to overcome the forces between them; particles separate and become a gas.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): accurate descriptions of all three states plus a clear explanation of boiling in terms of energy and forces
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct descriptions of the states with limited or no explanation of boiling
questions.explanation: Full answers describe both arrangement and movement for each state, then link boiling to energy overcoming forces between particles.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of sodium chloride and oxygen.
Explain the difference in melting points in terms of particles, bonding and energy.
Evaluate how well the simple particle model of solid spheres explains this difference.
markScheme: Indicative content: sodium chloride: giant ionic lattice; particles are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions; large amount of energy needed to overcome them; high melting point. Oxygen: small molecules (O₂); weak forces between molecules; little energy needed to overcome them; low melting point; covalent bonds are not broken. Stronger forces mean higher melting point. Evaluation (HT): the simple model shows particles as solid spheres with no forces between them, so it cannot explain why energy is needed or why the melting points differ; all particles are shown as identical spheres, but ions and molecules differ in size, shape and charge; real particles are not solid; the model is useful for showing arrangement and movement but not for explaining melting points.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logical explanation linking particles, bonding, forces and energy for both substances, with a reasoned evaluation of the model that identifies its limitations
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a correct explanation for both substances in terms of strength of forces, with limited evaluation of the model
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'sodium chloride has stronger bonds', with little explanation
questions.explanation: This combines 4.2.2.1 with the Higher-tier limitations. The key idea is that the model has no forces, yet forces are exactly what determine melting point.
